faq.a: Pregnancy increases iron demand and folate is needed for neural‑tube development; supplementation prevents anemia and birth defects.
faq.q: Why is iron‑folic acid given to every pregnant woman?

faq.a: It reduces maternal malaria episodes, anemia, and low birth weight by clearing parasites each trimester.
faq.q: What is the purpose of intermittent preventive treatment for malaria in pregnancy?

faq.a: If she has HIV, malaria, hypertension, diabetes, sickle cell disease, previous obstetric complications, or multiple gestation.
faq.q: When can a woman be classified as high‑risk and need extra ANC visits?

exam: What immediate investigations would you order for a 28‑week pregnant woman presenting with new‑onset headache and BP 150/95 mmHg? — Check BP twice, urine protein dipstick, and baseline labs (Hb, creatinine) to assess for pre‑eclampsia.

How does intermittent preventive treatment for malaria differ from treatment of an acute malaria episode? — IPT uses a single dose of SP each trimester for prophylaxis; acute malaria requires full ACT regimen.

A woman tests positive for syphilis at her first ANC visit. What is the recommended management and why? — Give benzathine penicillin 2.4 MU IM single dose; it prevents congenital syphilis and is safe in pregnancy.

Explain why ACE inhibitors are contraindicated in pregnancy and what alternative antihypertensives are preferred. — ACE inhibitors cause fetal renal dysgenesis; labetalol or nifedipine are safe choices.

During a routine visit you find a fundal height lagging by 4 cm. What are the possible causes and next steps? — Consider incorrect dating, fetal growth restriction, or oligohydramnios; repeat dating scan if possible, assess maternal nutrition and blood pressure.
Why should protease‑inhibitor based ART be avoided in a woman with severe liver disease? — Protease inhibitors are hepatotoxic; use tenofovir‑based regimen instead.

A pregnant woman with HIV is on cotrimoxazole prophylaxis. Which malaria prophylaxis should you avoid and why? — Avoid sulfadoxine‑pyrimethamine because of cross‑reactivity and risk of severe skin reactions.

What counselling points would you give to a woman who uses herbal remedies during pregnancy? — Discuss lack of safety data, potential uterotonic or teratogenic effects, and encourage evidence‑based supplements instead.
ai.title: Routine Antenatal Care
ai.subject: Obstetrics & gynaecology
ai.summary: Routine antenatal care (ANC) is a structured series of visits that monitor maternal and fetal health, provide preventive interventions, and identify complications early, especially in low‑resource settings.

b: Typically 8 contacts per WHO 2016 recommendation, but 4‑visit models are common where resources are limited
Diagnosis is clinical – confirmation of pregnancy by history, urine hCG or ultrasound when available
sections.p: ANC is a scheduled series of clinical contacts for a pregnant woman, beginning as early as possible, to assess health, screen for disease, and deliver preventive measures.

b: Low risk – no comorbidities, normal BMI, singleton, no previous obstetric complications
High risk – HIV, malaria, sickle cell disease, hypertension, diabetes, previous pre‑eclampsia, multiple gestation
sections.p: ANC itself is not staged, but risk stratification guides intensity of follow‑up.

b: Infectious: HIV, malaria, syphilis, hepatitis B, urinary tract infection
Non‑communicable: hypertension, anemia, diabetes, sickle cell disease
Social/Environmental: malnutrition, herbal medicine use, poor sanitation
sections.p: The main “causes” to anticipate are conditions that increase maternal or fetal risk and are common in East Africa.

b: History: gestational age, previous pregnancies, bleeding, pain, fever, urinary symptoms, drug use
Examination: blood pressure, weight, fundal height, fetal heart rate, edema, pallor
sections.p: Women attending for routine ANC are usually asymptomatic; the clinician must elicit hidden symptoms and perform focused examination.
Investigations are chosen to detect common maternal/fetal problems and to guide preventive therapy.

t.b: Screen for hypertension; ≥140/90 mmHg on two occasions 4 h apart indicates pre‑eclampsia risk
Detect anemia; Hb <11 g/dL in pregnancy suggests iron deficiency or other causes
Identify HIV infection; positive result triggers antiretroviral prophylaxis for mother and infant
Detect Plasmodium infection; positive result requires prompt ACT treatment
Protein ≥1+ suggests pre‑eclampsia; nitrites positive indicates urinary infection needing antibiotics
Identify active infection; positive result leads to penicillin treatment to prevent congenital syphilis
Screen for gestational diabetes; fasting ≥5.1 mmol/L or random ≥11.1 mmol/L warrants OGTT
Confirm gestational age, viability, number of fetuses, and major anomalies

b: Severe hypertension (≥160/110 mmHg) or new‑onset proteinuria
Heavy vaginal bleeding or sudden abdominal pain
Fever >38 °C with chills
Severe anemia (Hb <7 g/dL) or signs of heart failure
Rapidly rising fundal height with absent fetal heart sounds
sections.p: Identify early signs that require urgent referral or admission.

b: Intermittent preventive treatment for malaria (SP) in endemic areas, unless contraindicated
Daily sulfadoxine‑pyrimethamine for HIV‑positive women on cotrimoxazole prophylaxis is avoided
Antiretroviral therapy (tenofovir + lamivudine + efavirenz) for HIV‑positive mothers; avoid protease inhibitors in severe liver disease
Screen‑positive syphilis: single dose benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM
Hypertension: start labetalol or nifedipine; avoid ACE inhibitors in pregnancy
Gestational diabetes: dietary counseling, glucose monitoring; insulin if diet fails
sections.p: Management combines preventive interventions, treatment of identified conditions, and health education.

b: Low‑risk: visits at 12, 20, 28, 36 weeks (WHO 8‑contact model) or every 4 weeks if only four contacts possible
High‑risk: additional visits every 2 weeks or more often as indicated
Vaccination: tetanus toxoid (2 doses) and, where available, influenza vaccine
Counselling on nutrition, safe water, insecticide‑treated nets, and avoidance of harmful traditional medicines
sections.p: Schedule visits according to risk; reinforce health‑promoting behaviours.

b: Gestational hypertension vs chronic hypertension – differentiate by timing and prior history
Physiological edema vs pre‑eclampsia – look for proteinuria and BP rise
Mild anemia of pregnancy vs iron‑deficiency anemia – consider diet, malaria, hookworm
sections.p: Conditions that may mimic or be mistaken for routine ANC findings.

b: Hemoglobin may appear normal in malaria‑related hemolysis if measured early; repeat after treatment
Rapid HIV tests can give false‑negative results during acute infection – repeat after 4 weeks if high risk
Urine dipstick protein can be false‑positive after vigorous exercise or dehydration
